articles.title: Why India Needs a Common Drone Warfare Doctrine for All Three Services
articles.text:
India’s unmanned systems conversation has largely been a procurement conversation — how many Predator-derivative MQ-9B platforms the Navy and Air Force will operate, how quickly Archer-NG and other indigenous medium-altitude systems will reach squadron service, how many loitering munitions DRDO and private vendors can deliver against emergency procurement orders issued in the aftermath of recent border tensions. These are necessary questions. But they treat drones as individual platforms to be counted and inducted one airframe at a time, when the operational lesson from Ukraine, Nagorno-Karabakh, and India’s own recent experience along its borders points toward something different: the decisive capability is not the individual drone, it is coordinated mass.
A single loitering munition or reconnaissance drone is a useful tactical tool, easily countered by a competent air-defence network once detected. Dozens of coordinated drones, arriving from multiple axes with overlapping sensor coverage and autonomous target de-confliction, saturate exactly the kind of layered air-defence system that India’s adversaries have spent the past decade building along contested frontiers. The gap between these two employment concepts is not primarily a hardware gap. It is a doctrine and command-and-control gap, and it is the one India’s services have been slowest to close.
Building genuine swarm capability requires investment in three areas that individual platform procurement does not automatically deliver. The first is mesh networking and distributed autonomy software that lets a group of drones maintain coordinated behaviour even when individual links to a ground controller are jammed or degraded, rather than each drone depending on a continuous, individually-vulnerable control link. The second is a target de-confliction and tasking layer, almost certainly AI-assisted given the speed at which a saturating drone package needs to reassign targets among its constituent units, that operates at the swarm level rather than requiring a human operator to individually task each airframe. The third, and most institutionally difficult, is a doctrine and training pipeline within the Army, Navy, and Air Force that treats swarm employment as a distinct warfighting discipline, with its own tactics, its own dedicated units, and its own place in joint operational planning, rather than folding drone employment into existing artillery or air-defence force structures as an afterthought.
DRDO’s various loitering munition and unmanned systems programmes, alongside a genuinely vibrant private-sector drone industry that has emerged since 2020 policy liberalisation opened the sector to non-DPSU players, give India the hardware building blocks this doctrine would need. What is missing is the organisational decision to treat swarm employment as a standing capability requirement in its own right, with dedicated procurement lines for the networking and autonomy software layer, rather than assuming that buying enough individual drones will eventually and automatically produce swarm capability as a byproduct.
There is an export argument here too, echoing the pattern already visible with Turkey’s Baykar and its Bayraktar family. Countries that demonstrate genuine swarm doctrine, not merely individual drone sales, capture a premium in the international market that individual-platform vendors cannot match, because buyers are purchasing a warfighting concept and the training pipeline that comes with it, not just an airframe. If India wants its growing drone-manufacturing base to become a genuine export pillar rather than a domestic-substitution success story, doctrine has to lead hardware, not trail behind it as it largely does today.

articles.title: INS Samarthak Set to Become Indian Navy’s Drone Mothership
articles.text:
India’s newly commissioned IN Samarthak will play a key role in increasing the Indian Navy’s use of autonomous platforms and will have an array of functions including being a mothership for autonomous platforms and testing for new technology.
Built by Larsen & Toubro (L&T) at their Kattupalli shipyard near Chennai, the new ship has been commissioned on October 16th 2026 at Naval Base Karwar by Vice President C. P. Radhakrishnan. This is the first indigenous Multi-Purpose Vessel (MPV) built for the Indian Navy and is also the first significant warship to be built by a private shipbuilder in India.
The vessel will act as a mothership for autonomous and unmanned systems. The Ministry of Defence have stated that the vessel will be used for maritime surveillance, patrol, target laying, weapon and sensor experimentation, as well as humanitarian aid and disaster relief.
As seen in the L&T Precision Engineering and Systems presentation, the company produce a range of unmanned vehicles. As seen in the picture below, the vessel will be used for a range of autonomous systems including the AUV Maya X, Amogh and USV.
Autonomous Underwater Vehicles can complete underwater tasks without a crew while Unmanned Surface Vessels complete tasks on the surface. These can be used for seabed mapping, underwater surveying, surveillance, data gathering depending on their design and payloads.
Having a larger vessel to operate these vehicles from enables operations to occur outside of coast test facilities. The mothership can be used to deploy and recover platforms as well as providing logistical support, communication and testing of autonomous systems.
However, it cannot be confirmed from the L&T presentation that all of these vehicles will be operated from the INS Samarthak. The presentation shows what they are capable of. The vessel has been specifically designed for experimentation, this means the Navy can test new weapons, sensors and different systems. It has a dynamic positioning system which should help with accurate control during complex marine manoeuvres.
This vessel is reflective of the changes within the navy. There is a growing requirement for smaller autonomous platforms to be developed, alongside large warships which take longer to design, build and certify.
L&T have stated this presents a challenge for defence industry with the need to ensure reliable performance on major platforms but also speeding up development of small platforms that can be prototyped, experimented with and changed.

articles.title: Microsoft faces potential vote: Shareholders curious about its plans to tackle emissions
articles.text:
Trillium Asset Management wants Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets, and is backing a shareholder proposal to request this information at the firm’s next shareholder meeting.

The cloud and software biz set itself lofty environmental goals back in 2020, aiming to be become "carbon-negative" by 2030, and to have removed the equivalent of all the carbon it has ever emitted by 2050.

But since the start of the decade, an explosion in AI development and demand for ever more complex models has seen a boom in demand for high-performance compute infrastructure and a construction wave to deliver new datacenters to house it all in.

Microsoft is one of the firms to profit from this huge demand, with its cloud division making $214.4 billion in revenue for the fiscal year 2026 ended June 30, a 27 percent year-on-year increase.

This has also caused Microsoft’s emissions to head in the wrong direction, with figures from the company’s most recent Environmental Sustainability Report showing that these have increased from 13 million tons of CO2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025.

However, Microsoft estimates that without the carbon reduction initiatives it has already put in place, emissions would now be much higher, somewhere near 34 million tons.

The increase is largely accounted for by indirect emissions (Scope 3) from the construction and provisioning of datacenters to meet that demand for cloud services and AI training. But as The Register pointed out, 2025 saw a growing contribution from Scope 2, due to generation of energy the company purchased. This represents 13 percent of total emissions – up from 2 percent in 2024.

Now Trillium Asset Management, financial advisors specializing in sustainable and responsible investing, is urging Microsoft shareholders to vote for Proposal 4 during their annual meeting scheduled for December 8.

In an SEC filing, the proposal asks Microsoft to disclose additional information illustrating how it will manage climate commitments. This disclosure should go beyond existing disclosures, at reasonable cost, omitting proprietary information, and be made annually.

The proposal notes that when Microsoft first announced its carbon negative goal, it said progress required "not just a bold goal but a detailed plan," and that transparency was one of the guiding principles for this climate plan.

It states that emissions are now 62 percent above the 2020 baseline, and simply asks Microsoft to apply the principles it articulated in 2020; show the plan, be candid about the math, and explain how it will adapt.

In the filing, Trillium warns that falling short of its climate targets may create risk to Microsoft’s credibility, which can influence investor trust. If Microsoft is in danger of failing to meet its 2030 commitments, it could suffer reputational harm, and the filing claims it is already the subject of legal action by investors alleging insufficient disclosure of its AI and cloud spending.

On the flip side, it says that disclosure of a climate transition plan will likely prove valuable to large institutional investors who view climate change as a systemic risk to future economic growth.

We asked Microsoft for comment, but it already recommended in another SEC filing that shareholders vote against the proposal, arguing it fails to show that Microsoft’s existing disclosures are insufficient for investors to assess its climate-related strategy and performance.

Instead, the firm says that the proposal requests a collection of new disclosures that go beyond not just legal and regulatory requirements, but also established voluntary climate-reporting frameworks.

The proposal seeks hypothetical scenarios, contingency plans and other forward-looking information that is inherently uncertain and subject to change, Microsoft states, saying it will remain focused on its Sustainability Report and other environmental reporting while meeting any new disclosure mandates that may arise globally. ®

articles.title: BRICS Forum Backs UN Reforms, Condemns Pahalgam Terror Attack
articles.text:
The two-day conclave of the BRICS Parliamentary Forum on Tuesday adopted a joint declaration strongly condemning the 2025 Pahalgam attack and all acts of terrorism as it pledged to combat the menace in all its forms and manifestations and also stressed on non-intervention in the internal affairs of any country.
The joint declaration, announced by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, also condemned the imposition of unilateral economic and secondary sanctions saying such coercive measures have far reaching negative implications on human rights, including the right to development, health and food security of people.
The BRICS Parliamentary Forum supported a comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including its Security Council, saying this reform should make it more just, equitable, democratic, representative, effective, and efficient, better reflecting contemporary realities and the needs of the international community.
“We express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed. We condemn in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir (in Pahalgam) on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured.
“We reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens,” the declaration read.
The Forum said terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and that all those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law.
“We urge to ensure zero tolerance for terrorism and reject double standards in countering terrorism. We emphasise the primary responsibility of States in combating terrorism and that global efforts to prevent and counter terrorist threats must fully comply with their obligations under international law, including the Charter of the UN…,” it read.
The Forum said it looks forward to further deepening counter-terrorism cooperation and calls for an expeditious finalisation and adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism in the UN framework and concerted actions against all UN-designated terrorists and terrorist entities.
“We reaffirm our adherence to the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, non-intervention in internal affairs, and the peaceful settlement of international disputes, as enshrined in the United Nations Charter, as essential foundations for global stability, peace and development,” it said.
The Forum reaffirmed its unwavering support for the peaceful resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict based on the two-state solution, with the two States living side by side, in peace and security, in accordance with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions.
It asserted the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination, freedom, and an independent, sovereign State.
The Forum expressed deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in West Asia and, recalling the respective national positions, called for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation.
It strongly condemned all violations of international humanitarian law, including deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure, including in BRICS member states, as well as the denial or obstruction of humanitarian access and the targeting of humanitarian personnel.
Iran and United Arab Emirates, which are directly involved with the West Asia conflict, are members of the BRICS. Apart from India, other member nations of the BRICS are: Brazil, Russia, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia and South Africa.
The Forum underlined the need to address accountability for all violations of international humanitarian law.
“We recognise international efforts undertaken by BRICS members to promote respect for, adherence to, and effective implementation of international humanitarian law,” it said.
Recognising the urgency of addressing climate change, the BRICS parliamentary body calls for intensifying efforts, through dialogue and international cooperation, to implement nationally determined contributions, strengthen mitigation and adaptation efforts, with a view to achieving the objectives of the UNFCCC and the goals of its Paris Agreement as applicable.
The Forum acknowledge the transformative potential of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI) and information and communication technologies (ICTs).
“We emphasise the necessity of ensuring the open, safe, secure, stable, equitably accessible, peaceful and interoperable use and development of ICTs environment while respecting sovereignty and national security of each country. “In addition, promoting energy efficiency of AI systems, fostering AI science and innovation, leveraging AI for economic growth and social good and mitigating potential risks would be essential for promoting a just, fair, equitable and prosperous future of all countries, especially those of Global South,” it said.

articles.title: A hidden ocean change near Antarctica could have global consequences
articles.text:
The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say.

In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years.

The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen, a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India.

articles.title: Japan Eyes Indian Missile Ranges for Type-25 Missile Tests

NHK (Japan Broadcasting Corporation) had reported that Japan is looking to India for opportunities to train with long-range weapons and systems, such as its recently deployed Type-25 anti-ship missile and small attack drones, which could mark a new opportunity for Indo-Japanese defence collaboration.
On 27 October General Masayoshi Arai, Chief of Staff at Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force (JGSDF) confirmed Japanese personnel had travelled to India to look at the opportunities for training. It has previously been reported that defence officials from Japan visited missile testing sites and ranges in India during a visit in mid October.
A key aspect of this looks set to be the Type-25 Surface-to-Ship Guided Missile. This is a long-range weapon system derived from the Type-12 anti ship missile. It entered into service in March 2026 and has a range of approximately 1000km. Exact figures on the maximum range have not been published by the Japanese authorities.
Arai added that Japan is looking at options to ensure it has the correct training environment domestically and potentially internationally. These include looking at training in India. This should not be confused with Japan’s Type-25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile. However, there are wider opportunities for collaboration. Arai confirmed that small attack drone training is also being looked at.
Training would involve radio frequency considerations, appropriate training sites, and safe operating conditions. Details of what type of drones are being looked at have not been revealed. If an agreement is reached with India, this would offer Japan another opportunity to train with long-range weapons. The collaboration would also increase the practical collaboration between the two Indo-Pacific partners.
New Delhi would gain from this initiative as it would allow them to work alongside Japanese kit and technology. Collaborative training would help increase military interaction, understanding of each other’s processes and increase defence relations.
Japan has been increasing its stand-off capabilities due to concerns over China’s military activity in the western Pacific and around Taiwan. India has created a wide range of missile testing facilities, including on the eastern coast. Whether specific ranges in India could undertake the training would depend on whether they could technically support the training, ensure they are safe for the range and have the approvals.

articles.title: China's spaceplane bears striking resemblance to America's X-37B
articles.text:
China's secretive spaceplane has been spotted in orbit by a US commercial satellite, according to the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)

The DIA's report [PDF] warns of developments by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea that allegedly threaten space security, at least from a US perspective. Most of the report details systems still under development, but one image on page 53 stands out: China's spaceplane, snapped in orbit in 2024 by Maxar Technologies.

The image has been seen before; a low-resolution snap from an industry symposium was shared by Bluesky user @dutchspace almost two years ago. However, the higher-resolution image in the DIA report shows more detail. The spaceplane also bears a distinct resemblance to the US Space Force's X-37B.

The uncrewed X-37 began as a NASA project in 1999 before the US Department of Defense took over. After several atmospheric tests with an X-37A variant, the X-37B was launched in 2010. The reusable spaceplane can spend years in orbit, conducting classified activities. So far, it has launched eight times.

According to the DIA's report, China's first spaceplane mission launched in 2020 and remained in orbit for two days. A second, launched in 2022, spent 276 days in orbit, and a third, launched in December 2023, spent 268 days in oribt. The last two missions appeared to include approach and rendezvous tests of objects in orbit.

Russia, memorably, had a spaceplane in the ill-fated Buran, which bore an uncanny resemblance to the US Space Shuttle (although the two were very different beasts from a technical perspective – not least, Buran's orbiter did not carry the engines used to launch it to space).

However, according to the DIA's report, Russia "has made little progress since."

The US recently confirmed that it has weapons in space, and it would be naive not to assume rivals would have their own, whether kinetic or some form of jamming technology.

articles.text:
Intel has become the latest target for Good Jobs First, which questions why the chipmaker continues to receive tax breaks from key states, long after setting up shop there, and laying off thousands of workers in those regions.

The non-profit organization, which promotes accountability in economic development, says the chipmaker promised billions of dollars in investment and thousands of high-tech jobs for the areas surrounding its manufacturing plants in Hillsboro, Oregon, and Rio Rancho, New Mexico.

Its report, The Bleeding Edge: How the Public Pays the Costs of Intel’s Semiconductor Manufacturing, claims that Intel's property tax breaks cost these communities more than $1.2 billion in lost revenue since 2015, and the brunt of the shortfall has largely fallen on schools funded by those local governments.

For Oregon, Good Jobs First says that property tax abatements from Intel's use of the Strategic Investment Program (SIP) exempted it from at least $1.14 billion, while Hillsboro schools lost $891 million in revenue from 2017 through 2025.

During the same timeframe, Intel paid Oregon $552.4 million in fees, or less than a third of the value of its tax breaks.

In New Mexico, the figures are lower, but still significant. The report puts Chipzilla's property tax exemptions from Industrial Revenue Bonds (IRBs) at $99.6 million in foregone revenue since 2017, while Rio Rancho’s Public Schools lost an estimated $43.4 million over the same nine-year period. Here, the company paid $41.6 million in required payments in lieu of taxes from 2017 through 2025, shared among affected local governments.

Good Jobs First also notes that despite these subsidies, Intel was awarded billions under the CHIPS Act funding from the US federal government.

However, the situation with that is somewhat complex, as the company secured an initial $7.86 billion under the Biden administration, of which $2.2 billion is believed to have been paid out.

The incoming Trump administration, however, decided to rethink the scheme, and ended up making an $8.9 billion deal for 10 percent of Intel’s common stock, made up of the remaining $5.7 billion of the CHIPS Act cash plus an additional $3.2 billion under the Secure Enclave program to make semiconductors for the military.

At the same time, the chipmaker is estimated by Good Jobs First to have laid off more than 4,700 workers at its facilities in Oregon and New Mexico over the past three years, as the company wrestled with restructuring efforts and dramatic losses.

(These are just a fraction of Intel’s total layoffs during the period.)

The issue, according to the non-profit, is that these sites are established Intel facilities which the company has operated for decades. They already have the facilities, infrastructure, skilled workers, and other necessities that a new site might require investment for. Are continued tax breaks truly necessary, Good Jobs First asks, or are they just subsidizing business decisions Intel would make anyway?

It says Intel’s track record in Oregon and New Mexico should be taken as important lessons for other communities considering becoming a home to semiconductor manufacturing, and recommends questioning whether state and local tax breaks are even necessary.

"Tax incentives are supposed to encourage investment, not provide companies with an ongoing stream of public support for decades," said Good Jobs First Research Analyst and report author Kristan Wong Karinen.

"Intel has received tax breaks at these campuses for generations, and local leaders should be asking hard questions about why those subsidies are still necessary, especially with the billions of dollars in federal grants and tax credits they receive from the CHIPS Act."

We asked Intel for a statement regarding these claims by Good Jobs First, and in response it told us: "Intel works closely with governments in the regions where we operate to leverage incentives that support leading-edge semiconductor R&D and manufacturing. We are not providing additional details beyond what's available in our annual reports."

Recent targets for the non-profit have been datacenters, and the states offering tax incentives for developers and operators to build within their jurisdiction. Some states were losing billions in lost revenue to server farm projects, while others were failing to disclose their tax shortfall. ®

Prime Toolings, an Indian manufacturing and propulsion technology company, is making significant strides in the development of advanced propulsion systems, with a focus on indigenous Rotating Detonation Engine (RDE) technology for next-generation aerospace and defence applications.

Prime Toolings has undertaken multiple research and development initiatives in collaboration with the Indian Navy, focusing on the potential of advanced propulsion technologies for future operational requirements.
The company aims to develop propulsion solutions that can reduce overall system dimensions, simplify storage requirements, and improve deployment readiness. Its long-term vision is to provide compact, integrated propulsion systems that can be stored efficiently and prepared for operation with minimal complexity.
Through its work on air-breathing and non-air-breathing RDE systems, Prime Toolings is investigating propulsion architectures that could offer new possibilities for compact aerospace and defence platforms.

The company’s broader objective is to establish an indigenous propulsion ecosystem capable of supporting India’s evolving aerospace and defence requirements.

AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models

When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data.

He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Are we there yet? Interspecies communication 

Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. 

Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex.


Find out how close we are to interspecies communication.

articles.title: Putin Revives Su-57 Joint Production Offer as FGFA Concerns Linger
articles.text:
Statements made by Russian President Vladimir Putin that India did not take up an opportunity to build the Su-57 in partnership have sparked renewed debate over the collapse of the Fifth Generation Fighter Aircraft (FGFA) agreement between the two nations. But the decision came after years of disagreements over technology sharing, build share, performance and cost.
Speaking to journalists in St Petersburg in June 2026, Putin said that the opportunity was given to India to build the fifth generation aircraft in partnership with Russia but New Delhi chose to delay. Russia went ahead with development and are now open to partnering on the project. Moscow has also put forward the opportunity to provide the Su-57 and potentially partner with India.
An Intergovernmental Agreement was signed in October 2007 between India and Russia to develop and produce a fifth generation aircraft together. A contract to begin the preliminary design phase of the aircraft was signed in December 2010.
However, in 2018 India exited the FGFA project as critical disagreements could not be resolved through negotiations. Concerns were raised about what India would get out of the deal.
A detailed analysis published in 2018 by the Vivekananda International Foundation showed that India had contributed around $295 million to the preliminary development stage. But the final build share was far less than originally planned with India having equal engineering and IP sharing.
India wanted to get involved in aspects such as mission computers, navigation, cockpit displays and countermeasure systems. In the end India had around 25% design of components and 15% of research and development. There was also disagreements with India wanting access to more sensitive software and source codes, allowing them to upgrade and maintain the aircraft independently. This led to lengthy negotiations and additional costs for the Indian side to gain access to computer codes.
Another significant challenge was the costs. The analysis shows that development costs were estimated to be billions of dollars. Then there was the potential cost of purchasing the actual aircraft.
A commonly cited issue is that India could have purchased two Rafale’s with their initial contribution, however this is misleading as the $295 million was spent on preliminary development. Although Putin’s latest offer may lead to renewed talks on the project, any new deal would have to be considered on its own merits. India would need clear details on what capabilities the aircraft would have, what technology would be transferred over, what would be indigenously manufactured, access to software, IP rights, authority to upgrade and how much the development and purchase would cost in total.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

Cisco open sources tool for detecting AI agents on hacking sprees
articles.text:
Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging Face hack – or worse.

It’s called Project Quarry, and it aims to provide a “shared language” for evaluating agent behavior, along the lines of what Snort, which Cisco also maintains, did for detecting malicious network traffic and what YARA did for rule-based malware identification.

Most detection tools rely on specific interactions with an AI model or agent. Did it attempt prompt injection? Or did the agent call an attack tool?

“But what is missing is the entire context under which something may occur,” Amy Chang, head of AI threat and security research at Cisco, said in an exclusive interview with The Register.

She likened this to credit card fraud detection. Without context, individual transactions such as a small test charge or a single purchase in a location far away from a card-holder's usual location may not raise any flags.

“And then you try again,” making another fraudulent purchase, “and that went through, too. So now I’m gonna buy the PS5,” Chang said.

“Those are the things that Quarry addresses by taking into consideration the entire agent session,” she explained. “One tool call may seem in-scope until you realize that that next step is taking that information and sending it to an attacker-controlled inbox or server.”

Even data theft is a sequence and not a single agentic action. Agentic AI security firm Invariant Labs demonstrated this with a proof-of-concept attack against GitHub's MCP server that hijacked a user's agent via a malicious GitHub Issue, and coerced it into leaking data from private repositories.

Simply reading a configuration file, or sending a request to an external endpoint may be legitimate agentic actions. However, combining the two can lead to data exfiltration – and shows “why action relationships matter,” wrote Chang and fellow Cisco researchers Adam Swanda, Ravikumar Balakrishnan, and Konstantin Berlin in a blog post about Quarry shared with The Register ahead of publication

“A policy can produce a finding when the trace shows a sensitive file read followed within a defined window by an external send,” they wrote. “The risk comes from the relationship between the two actions, so the finding should preserve evidence from both."

Quarry covers single- and multi-turn large language model conversations, agents, tool use, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, and multimodal inputs.

In addition to the open source code itself, the project’s GitHub repository includes installation instructions, supported Python versions, plugins for Claude Code, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents, configuration examples, rule-writing guidance, and a rule starter pack.

For instance, with the rule pack, “If a base-64 encoded malware is somewhere in the tool call, that would result in a block,” Chang said.

The rule format looks similar to a YARA or Snort rule, with a header that details the traffic to examine, content to match, and metadata for tracking the rule. Here’s a Quarry rule that flags an agent that reads a credentials file:

While the Cisco Ai researchers have not run Quarry against data describing the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, they suggest that if the intrusion had been read as a complete, step-by-step record of a single session, there were several points where the AI agents’ steps would have given a Quarry rule something to act on and flag for humans.

For example, Quarry would probably have flagged internet access from a sandbox.

“The rule can flag specific tool calls that reach an external server asset that wasn’t in the task’s allow list,” Chang said.

“Another one would be credentials found and used somewhere else.”

According to OpenAI’s technical report about the Hugging Face intrusion, this is exactly what happened on July 10, when an agent validated 14 exposed Hugging Face tokens with write access and shared them.

“The rule would flag that there was a credential in the tool result that then called an outside service, which is likely not within the parameters of what you would want to do in this case,” Chang said. “We don't want you to go and search for credentials that may have been leaked or inadvertently exposed and then utilize them to conduct a task.”

The Cisco team is quick to say that rules along are not a substitute for chain-of-thought monitors, or other forms of human oversight – but they do help record a pattern that other teams can then “review, test, and apply to their own agents,” they wrote.

Herein also lies the benefit of open source, and a collective approach to defending against adversarial use of AI, Chang said.

“Do we have all the answers? No,” Chang said. “We all see slices of the problem, and it’s important for us to share what we see.”®
articles.summary: Cisco has open sourced a behavior detection engine that watches AI agents, to help security teams prevent rogue agents from going off the rails like they did with the Hugging Face hack – or worse.<

articles.title: 123 Reg discloses 'AI cyberattack' on customer data, suspects China nexus
articles.text:
UK domain registrar 123 Reg (no relation – Ed) says it was the victim of an “AI-driven cyberattack” that exposed customer data.

Customers began receiving their notification emails this week, informing them that their contact information, "related customer relationship data," company VAT numbers, and "product information from an application programming interface (API)" were compromised.

A company spokesperson elaborated, saying this means that names, phone numbers, countries, language and currency preferences, account creation dates, the products on the account, and marketing preferences were affected.

123 Reg described the September 18 intrusion as "the first known AI-driven cyberattack against our company," and told The Register that early signs point toward a China-nexus attacker.

"Our investigation identified IP addresses that we assessed to be the core attacker infrastructure, which were hosted in China and Singapore, indicating a strong Chinese nexus," the spokesperson said. 

"Our investigation further identified AI cyberattack 'skills' hosted on Chinese infrastructure, including copies of skills open sourced by Anthropic and several other AI exploitation frameworks and scripts."

They went on to say that many of the artefacts left behind led 123 Reg to suspect that a Chinese state-sponsored group, known for abusing Claude Code in attacks against at least 30 organizations, could be behind the break-in.

There is also a suspicion that the same group that hit a number of South Korea’s financial institutions using open-source Chinese AI tool ARTEX, was behind the attack on 123 Reg too.

"The TA's mirror of 'anthropic_skills,' and the account naming conventions found on the Chinese servers are consistent with preparation of this class of AI-augmented operation," the spokesperson told us. 

"In addition, on October 7, 2026, CrowdStrike published CSA-261162, describing an unknown, likely Chinese-speaking actor that targeted several South Korean financial organizations starting in late September 2026, which is the same period during which we were attacked.

"That actor used ARTEX, an open-source Chinese-developed agentic penetration-testing tool released in July 2026, which was also observed to be used in the attack that targeted us."

The GoDaddy-owned registrar reported the attack to law enforcement agencies, brought in outside cybersecurity support, and notified the FTC, as well as the data protection authorities in the UK and EU.

The company spokesperson added that it worked with Singapore-based ISPs to shut down the attacker's servers in the region, which helped disrupt the attack, in addition to "other actions by us and industry partners."

123 Reg's email to customers stated the attacker's activity "was limited to reading" customer data, although the spokesperson told us "it's possible they created copies of the information," and that this is what prompted the notification.

The registrar urged customers to stay alert to the potential misuse of their data, and to treat communications appearing to come from the company with caution.

"If you receive a message or call and aren't sure it's from 123 Reg, go directly to our website and log in," the email said. "We will never contact you to request your password, payment details, or verification codes by email, text, or phone.

"We also strongly recommend turning on two-step verification (2SV), which helps keep your account protected even if someone tricks you into sharing your password. You can find instructions for setting up 2SV in your 123 Reg account.

"We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused." ®

The question of who controls satellite-based connectivity came into sharp focus in recent weeks after Ukraine's service was throttled and then restored.

Wherever Reg readers stand on those activities involving SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield, reliance on a foreign power that may not stay friendly is now under intense scrutiny. Alternatives exist, including Eutelsat OneWeb's constellation, and more are in the works. The Register toured the Harwell facility of another contender – Open Cosmos.

The business is just over a decade old and operates from multiple locations, including the UK, Greece, and Portugal. It has launched dozens of missions over the years, including its OpenConstellation service, which organizations use to share data from Earth observation satellites.

When it launched OpenConstellation in 2022, the aim was to have 25 satellites offering a mix of spatial and spectral resolution. While other services, such as the European Commission's Copernicus, provide similar data, OpenConstellation lets customers assign satellites specific tasks for specific data collection.

However, it is ConnectedCosmos that will interest users concerned about putting all their connectivity eggs in a basket that might be abruptly snatched away. The first two satellites in the constellation are now in orbit; they were launched by Rocket Lab in January 2026. The business plans to operate more than 96 satellites by the end of 2028 and to achieve full coverage by 2030. The core connectivity backbone will consist of 192 satellites, which founder and CEO Rafel Jordà Siquier described as "the foundation, not the ceiling."

The company reckons it can churn out one satellite per day, and judging by what we saw in Harwell, that figure seems realistic, though it's a far cry from the approximately 70 Starlinks per week SpaceX claimed in its IPO filing.

Because ConnectedCosmos operates from an altitude above 1,000 km, it needs far fewer satellites, though at the cost of latency increases.

Jordi Barrera Ars, co-founder and CTO, told us that latency was "anything between 30 and 80 milliseconds." This is OK for most applications, but not great for some. Direct to smartphone is, for example, not currently on the cards. Open Cosmos's VP of Commercial Satcom, Danielle Edwards, said, "We're very much in the direct device business. Direct to smartphone is not an area that we have an interest in right now."

"Never say never…" she added, "and who knows what might come along next Tuesday. But for right now, the direct device play really is on the IoT side."

During the tour, Open Cosmos showed off its assembly and testing facilities (including temperature and pressure testing), as well as a shaker table that simulates launch conditions. The satellites themselves consist of a common bus, onto which solar panels and the payload are fitted. Then they are stored, ready for launch, in what one company representative called "the satellite nursery".

The approach is interesting: OpenConstellation satellites use the ConnectedCosmos constellation as a connectivity backbone, while the latter also provides point-to-point broadband. According to Open Cosmos:

"The constellation is deliberately designed around the requirements of government, institutional and commercial customers that need secure, resilient connectivity and clear custody of critical data."

It is very much a European alternative to customers who are worried about existing services.

The service on offer from Open Cosmos will not, for example, be suitable for guiding drones traveling at high velocities, that isn't really the point, but it will provide sovereign communication channels that aren't beholden to the whim of a man and a big, red Off switch. Where the Starlink constellation stands at well over 10,000 satellites, the numbers proposed by Open Cosmos are far more modest and less likely to alarm astronomers in quite the same way.

Plus, the company has sector experience through its OpenConstellation platform (as well as custom spacecraft built for individual customers). And, unlike so many in the industry, its satellites and facilities exist beyond PowerPoint presentations. After all, we've seen them. ®

articles.title: Man spends 35 years collecting corporate waffle, turns it into an app
articles.text:
After suffering more than 10,000 corporate meetings, one executive has decided that the world hasn't endured nearly enough management jargon and built an app capable of generating 270 million variations of it.

Dave Doty, who claims to have spent 35 years collecting buzzwords, clichés, and other verbal atrocities inflicted on office workers, turned his life's work into Executive Eightball, an iPhone and Android app designed to help users sound convincingly corporate while saying nothing.

The idea came about after Doty spent decades recording the nonsense he heard in meetings, presumably while everyone else was busy circling back, touching base, and taking things offline.

"I am an executive who has suffered through over 10,000 meetings during the course of my 30-year career," Doty told The Register. "To keep my sanity, in each of them, I wrote down all of the buzz words and business clichés and have built an enormous database of them."

He described his creation as "sort of what would happen if Dilbert and George Costanza had a love child."

The app, which is now available on Apple's App Store and Google Play, takes Doty's collection of corporate waffle and assembles it into sentences that wouldn't look out of place in a CEO's quarterly update or a particularly painful all-hands meeting.

Among the pearls of wisdom it can produce are "We must dashboard the outputs to enable us to focus on operational directives and break the paradigm" and "Drive to cross-functional synergies so we can reengineer the organization and unleash shareholder value."

Doty claims Executive Eightball can produce approximately 270 million unique sentences in 15 languages, meaning workers across the globe can now contribute to meetings without the tiresome business of having an actual idea.

The app's listing promises to help users "Speak fluent corporate nonsense instantly," with suggested applications including office humor, LinkedIn jokes, presentation icebreakers, and, perhaps most appropriately, "Fake CEO energy."

There's a free version, although you'll have to put up with ads and a limited supply of corporate waffle. For $0.99, you can unlock the lot and talk complete rubbish to your heart's content.

The timing is rather fitting. In March, research covered by The Register suggested that people who enthusiastically embrace corporate buzzwords may actually be worse at their jobs. Now there's an app to help the rest of us catch up.

Doty, meanwhile, appears delighted with his contribution to the corporate world.

"This is truly a paradigm shift for corporate leadership and my greatest lifetime contribution to society," he wrote in his latest email, urging potential customers to subscribe to the paid version to "unleash the value."

After 35 years and 10,000 meetings, at least someone has finally found a productive use for all that wasted time. ®

articles.title: Neocloud thinks AI agents - not meatbags - will be its main customers
articles.text:
Newly formed Quake AI is a cloud provider that expects its users will be mostly agents rather than humans.

It was created after US-based Rumble Inc acquired German datacenter operator Northern Data in June. The parent then rebranded as RUM Group, a holding company for Quake AI (formerly Northern Data) and the Rumble video platform.

Quake AI is an Nvidia Cloud Partner (NCP) operating a 22,000 GPUs estate, making it a neocloud: a specialized infrastructure provider dedicated to AI workloads.

Yet where other neoclouds are building a full stack of services around their GPU farms, Quake AI wants to make its infrastructure discoverable to AI agents, which may soon be traversing the internet in hordes on behalf of their owners.

RUM Group's chief financial officer Mike Massey told The Register that "Cloud 1.0 - let's call it applications - is like a user interface of how you interact with a machine of some kind."

He added: "Now, if you think about agents, they don't use vision. That's not how they interact with systems. They interact with APIs and with information effectively, and that means they want highly discoverable, highly data-driven platforms..

“So, to us, the things that make GPUs and AI compute easier to consume for humans, things like model-as-a-service, dashboards and one-click settings, are actually orthogonal to, if not detrimental to what agents are going to want, agents are going to want homogeneous compute… to understand and know what your data and your expectations are in terms of performance and uptimes, and then they're going to want to consume that compute as a utility,” he claimed.

In other words, Quake AI believes that, at some point, the customers for its compute services are going to be AI agents rather than people, but carrying out tasks on their behalf.

“I think that is the case, and it's the vision that we are driving towards, and you know ultimately agents are in service of people, right?” Massey said.

In its view of things, agents won't go through an intermediary, they'll go to the compute to retrieve the answers they need. "So all of these tool frameworks and all of these things that we have set up, I think, are a hindrance or an encumbrance to what the agents are going to want to consume, which is a utility," he explained.

"Yes, we're a little crazy in this regard," Massey added. "It's different. But I think our worldview is very grounded in the data and the realities. Like, we're a technical team. We understand the engineering, and at the end of the day, I think that most would validate our hypothesis," he continued.

John Hoffman, CEO of Northern Data and acting CEO of Quake AI, compared this with a solution he had been shown of an AI that was developed to navigate the internet by itself.

"I told it I wanted pizza. It went on to DoorDash's website. Typed pizza in the search box, clicked on the pizza with the highest ranking, went to add to order, knows I like pepperoni, and it clicked through all of this," he said.

"Don't get me wrong, this was a good solution that solves the problem. But the amount of compute that you are using to try to get an AI agent to act like a human that has eyes that can see web links is insanity compared to if DoorDash just created an API that is queryable," Hoffman claimed.

Done that way, the compute usage would be one thousandth of the way that the problem was actually accomplished, Quake AI claims, but it will require that everybody embraces the idea of how agents interact.

"And they don't interact with interfaces or applications. They interact with data and APIs. Just give me the raw data. That's what it wants," Hoffman told us.

"I would imagine DoorDash is developing an API for agents," he added. "It just makes sense, and that’s why we're doing the same exact thing."

Earlier this year, TollBit, an outfit that tracks AI bot traffic, said that agents were gradually taking over the internet. Its State of the Bots report found that by the end of 2025, there was roughly one AI bot visit for every 31 human visits to a site, up from just one for every 200 human visits at the start of the year.

Last year, consultants McKinsey & Company produced a report saying that the neocloud operators had to evolve beyond being just a provider of GPUs-as-a-service and move up the AI stack to sell services on top of bare metal, or risk being commoditized into competing on price.

Analyst firm Gartner was also reading the last rites for much of the neocloud industry recently, forecasting that AI services are unlikely to deliver enough revenue to cover the expected capital expenditure on IT infrastructure between now and 2030, and that consolidation in the provider market was inevitable.

Quake AI's gamble is that AI agents will be a reality, and that by tailoring its APIs to make it easier for these autonomous software bots to access its resources as needed, it will be one of the winners. ®

articles.title: Why roaming packages have become an anachronism in the age of app-first travel
articles.text:
Travelling in the modern day and age differs significantly from what it looked like a few short decades ago. Today, it is all about apps: you need applications for navigation, booking accommodation, buying tickets for events, following the local news, staying in touch with friends and family, and more. That also means that you depend on connectivity at all times while abroad.

The problem is that a lot of people still rely on traditional roaming, while the roaming model is out of date. You cannot choose a specific mobile internet plan that suits your travel plans. Instead, operators have split the world into zones, and each zone has its own pricing, limits, and permissions.

That is why many have turned to alternative ways of staying connected, and so far, the travel eSIM has emerged as the most practical solution. Companies like the Swiss eSIM pioneer, Yesim, have recognized the problem that travelers are facing and have come up with a solution. They let you pick a specific plan that will fit your trip. That way, you get to tailor your connectivity experience in advance. Furthermore, you even get to see the price in advance and know exactly what you will have to pay.

Home-operator roaming: Connectivity under outdated rules

The problem with roaming is that your home operator decides what your internet will be like abroad. When you try to book a flight or a hotel room, you will try to get the best deal possible. That means comparing providers, prices, any potential benefits that different providers offer, and the like. However, with roaming, you can’t do any of that. The terms of your existing home contract still apply, and connectivity abroad just gets added to it.

That means that your operator decides what zones are available, what partner networks you can access, and, most importantly, how much they will charge you. You, as the user, can only accept their terms or choose to look for a different way to secure an internet connection. In other words, there is no flexibility and no participation on your end, you can only take it or leave it.

Take EE as an example - the official terms for their EE Travel Data pass for Canada and the US say that the user gets 500 MB of data per day. This is not nearly enough for someone who will depend on their phone for everything, from paying for food to comparing ticket prices and booking accommodation. The limit is the same for countless other countries, including Australia, China, India, Mexico, New Zealand, South Africa, Thailand, Turkey, and the UAE.

It gets even worse for other countries, including Japan, Singapore, South Korea, and Indonesia. For these, the daily allowance is only 150 MB. That essentially forces you to ration your data use very carefully and pick what you are going to use it for.

Some providers have introduced daily packages as a secondary roaming option. O2 Travel Bolt On roaming option for Pay Monthly customers charges £7 for every 24 hours of use. They start charging you as soon as you make a call, send a text, or use data for anything. It happens even if your phone updates an app automatically in the background, without you even knowing about it.

As a result, you get barely any connectivity, but still have to pay the full price of this deal. For some, that might be fine, but if you aren’t aware of it, you can return home to a surprise bill that you now have to pay.

Travel eSIM as an alternative to roaming: Choice and control pass to the user

As mentioned, travel eSIM emerged as an alternative to the roaming model. The first thing to note about it is the difference between an eSIM and a travel eSIM.

An eSIM is a chip that is built into most modern smartphones, tablets, and similar devices. This chip allows users to install operator profiles offered by travel eSIM providers. This can be done remotely, without having to go to the provider’s shop. It’s as simple as downloading an app.

Travel eSIM uses this chip to create a digital service. That typically includes the provider’s app, tariffs, partnered mobile networks, full control of your data, and even top-ups and customer support, should you need them.

The system is also quite practical, as you get to set up everything in advance. You don’t have to wait to enter another country to secure your connectivity, but can instead do it from home before you leave on your trip. Start by checking your device’s compatibility with eSIM technology. If it’s compatible, you can download the operator’s app, pick a package for the region you plan to visit, and install the appropriate profile. Then, sit on the plane, travel to your destination, and activate the profile when you get there. You get instant connectivity without having to stand in line at a SIM kiosk, rely on Wi-Fi coverage, or pay high roaming prices.

If you are still not sure if a travel eSIM is the right option, consider the following: A one-week trip from the UK to the US will have you paying £7 per day if you are an O2 Travel user. For seven days abroad, that will end up being £49. Alternatively, if you use Yesim’s unlimited package for the US for seven days, the price is only £18.27 as of the time of writing. You buy it upfront, and it won’t activate until you start using it after arriving at your destination.

Travel eSIM fits the app-first logic of travel

When selecting a plan, you start with the trip itself. In other words, you click on the country or region that you plan to visit. You can also enter the length of your stay there, and how much data you expect you will need. Then, select a tariff to match the parameters.

All terms of the deal will be known to you in advance, including the country that is covered by the plan, how long the plan will last, how much data you get, and how much it all costs. Best of all, everything is managed in the app, so you don’t really have to get in contact with anyone.

A package can be selected for a single country, an entire region, or a route that includes several countries. You prepare all of this at home, and activate it after arrival. You even get to keep your home number active, since you don’t have to replace your SIM card. That way, any banking messages, service notifications, important calls, 2-Factor Authentication (2FA) texts, and the like can come through and reach you at any time.

Yesim: The Swiss standard for travel connectivity

If you need a travel eSIM provider, consider the Swiss company Yesim. The firm has been in the travel eSIM market since 2019, becoming one of the pioneers in this sector. Today, it provides connectivity to over 4 million users across 200+ destinations. For travelers, this means that they can rely on one service that they are familiar with regardless of whether they are going on a short holiday in one country or a lengthy, complex trip that will include multiple nations.

Yesim’s position as a global provider of connectivity services is also reflected in the fact that the company has become an official partner of the World Players Super League - the largest golf tour in the world. The League holds over 1,800 tournaments in more than 50 countries every year, and is one of the largest events of this kind.

The same global scale is evident in Yesim’s pricing options. The firm offers a flexible tariff range, especially when it comes to its most popular packages. For example, the Global Package covers 80+ countries, while the Global Plus Package covers 140+ destinations. These will likely suit those who tend to travel a lot and want to pay a fixed budget. But, if your data needs are unpredictable, you can always pick the Pay & Fly tariff - Yesim’s pay-as-you-go model. This is a single eSIM for 170+ countries, and you only pay for the data that you actually used.

Yesim’s offer is known for the ease and simplicity of connection. The firm has created an intuitive app where you simply pick a country or a region, install the profile, and activate it in a few taps after getting there. Plus, the app uses automatic network selection. This is possible thanks to SwitchLess Networks technology, which switches the user to the strongest available network at any given time. This is especially important for remote locations, where connectivity is usually unstable, but it can also come in handy for mass events, when the network may struggle to cope with tens of thousands of connections at once.

Yesim also offers the Multiple eSIMs feature, which helps you manage several profiles from a single account. This is convenient for those traveling with their family or a small group. You can even test its service with a trial plan that gives you 500 MB for a symbolic price of £0.45. That way, you can see how it all works for yourself before committing any real money. Lastly, Yesim offers a 15 percent discount to new users who use promocode GETYESIM15, so make sure to use it.

Conclusion

Since modern travel has evolved and is now an app-first experience, the old roaming model is no longer a good fit for an average traveler. Instead, travel eSIMs give tourists the freedom to choose their location, amount of data, and even to know the cost upfront. Yesim is a prime example of the fact that the travel eSIM model works and that it can satisfy the needs of modern-day travellers.

"For Yesim, freedom of connectivity is a fundamental human right that helps people stay close, communicate, and share meaningful moments in spite of distance," emphasizes the company's founder and CEO, Dmitri Verbovski.
